properties.natural_language: Before updating the finalized epoch metric, an epoch transition must have occurred and the finalized checkpoint must reference a valid epoch number that is monotonically non-decreasing relative to the previous finalized epoch.
The finalized epoch metric must always be less than or equal to the current justified epoch metric, reflecting the consensus invariant that finality follows justification.
The Prometheus metrics endpoint must only be accessible to authorized monitoring infrastructure; exposure to untrusted parties would disclose validator counts, sync state, and peer topology.
Metric collection overhead must remain negligible relative to consensus processing time; metric instrumentation must not delay block processing or attestation validation.
Metrics labeled as gauges but describing cumulative totals (e.g., attestations_received_total) must be treated as counters that are monotonically non-decreasing within an epoch.
After fork choice runs, if a reorg is detected, the reorg counter must be incremented exactly once and the head slot metric must reflect the new chain head.
Each data column sidecar submitted for gossip verification must pass batched KZG commitment verification and inclusion proof verification before being counted as a processing success.
Reconstruction of missing data columns must only use data from columns that have passed full KZG and inclusion proof verification; unverified column data must never be used in reconstruction.
After metric collection at epoch transition, the reported collection event timestamp must correspond to the actual epoch boundary, even if the underlying value accumulates continuously per-slot.

A received block must pass full header validation (parent hash, gas limit within parent +/- 1/1024 and >= 5000, timestamp > parent, difficulty per formula, extra data <= 32 bytes) before any ommer validation or body execution occurs.
Block must contain at most 2 ommers, each with age between 1 and 6 blocks, no duplicates, and valid parent references in the recent canonical chain.

After applying the block body, the computed state root, transaction root, receipt root, and logs bloom must exactly match the values declared in the block header; any mismatch must cause block rejection.

A transaction must satisfy all of: available gas in block >= tx.gas, sender nonce == account nonce exactly, sender balance >= tx.gas * tx.gas_price + tx.value, and sender account has no code (is EOA).
Total ETH is conserved across each transaction: gas_fee_paid_to_miner + gas_refunded_to_sender + value_transferred = gas_deducted_upfront + value_deducted, with no net creation or destruction of ETH.

After transaction execution, the sender's nonce must be exactly one greater than before, the gas refund must be min(gas_used/2, refund_counter), and a receipt must be generated with correct cumulative gas and logs bloom.
The Ethash PoW algorithm must be cryptographically secure against pre-computation; the hashimoto_light result must be deterministic for given inputs and the mix_digest must match the computed value.
After PoW verification passes, the result must satisfy result <= MAX_VALUE / difficulty and the difficulty must follow the Homestead formula including the ice age bomb: 2^(block_number/100000 - 2).
The block gas limit must be within parent_gas_limit +/- parent_gas_limit/1024 and must be >= 5000 (GAS_LIMIT_MINIMUM).
After block finalization, the miner must receive exactly 5 ETH + (5 ETH / 32) * ommer_count, and each ommer miner must receive exactly ((8 - ommer_age) * 5 ETH) / 8.
Nonce mismatch must result in transaction rejection from the current block but not permanent ban; the transaction may be re-submitted with the correct nonce.
Honest miners must control sufficient hash power to prevent 51% attacks; the security of block production relies on this majority assumption.
ECDSA signatures must be unforgeable: only the holder of the private key can produce a valid signature, ensuring no attacker can impersonate accounts.
Block timestamps must increase monotonically relative to the parent block; manipulation of timestamps would compromise difficulty adjustment correctness.
All RPC responses from third-party providers must include cryptographic proofs (Merkle proofs against known state roots); responses without proofs must be rejected.
After successful proof verification, the client must accept the data without requiring trust in the RPC provider; the data is cryptographically guaranteed authentic.
After proof verification fails, the data must be discarded and the provider must be flagged as potentially malicious; no unverified data may be used.
Light clients must have access to verified state roots (from consensus layer) to validate proofs; without trusted state roots the entire proof-based verification model is invalid.
SSZ Merkle proofs must be computationally unforgeable: an attacker cannot produce a valid proof for data that does not exist in the committed state.
After converting a transaction from RLP to SSZ format, the resulting SSZ hash tree root must uniquely identify the transaction and enable generation of partial proofs for individual fields.
After receipt normalization, all fields required for independent verification (logIndex, individual gasUsed) must be present and the receipt must be convertible to SSZ format.
Log query results must include completeness proofs demonstrating that no additional matching data exists beyond what was returned.
The 2D log index must provide bounded false-positive guarantees and the system must handle potentially expensive queries without enabling denial of service.
Backward compatibility must be maintained during the RLP-to-SSZ transition period; applications relying on current patterns must not break.
A deposit transaction must include pubkey (48 bytes), withdrawal_credentials (32 bytes), signature (96 bytes), and deposit_data_root; the ETH amount rounded to Gwei must meet MIN_DEPOSIT_AMOUNT.
The supplied deposit_data_root must match the computed SSZ hash tree root of the DepositData object; mismatched roots must cause the transaction to revert.
The deposit contract does NOT perform BLS signature verification; BLS verification is deferred entirely to the beacon chain. Invalid BLS signatures result in ETH being permanently burned.

After a deposit is accepted, the deposit leaf must be inserted into the incremental Merkle tree at depth 32 using O(log(n)) storage, and a DepositEvent must be emitted with pubkey, withdrawal_credentials, amount, signature, and index.
When the beacon chain processes a deposit, it must perform full BLS12-381 signature verification; deposits with invalid signatures must be silently ignored without affecting chain state.
The progressive Merkle tree supports up to 2^32 deposits (DEPOSIT_CONTRACT_TREE_DEPTH=32); exceeding this would corrupt the deposit root.
Any 32-byte value is accepted as withdrawal_credentials by the deposit contract; semantic validation of the prefix byte is deferred to beacon chain processing.
The beacon chain must eventually process all valid deposits emitted as DepositEvent logs; failure to do so would result in permanent fund loss.
An attacker cannot front-run a legitimate deposit to change the deposit_data_root validation outcome; deposit ordering must not affect root validation.
At every opcode boundary during EVM execution: gas_left + gas_consumed = initial_gas. No gas is created or destroyed during execution; the gas accounting is always balanced.
Before contract creation, the target address must be checked for collision: if the address already has code or nonce > 0, creation must fail with AddressCollision error.
After init code execution, the output runtime code must pass validation: size <= MAX_CODE_SIZE and must not start with byte 0xEF. Invalid code must trigger rollback of all state changes.
After successful contract deployment, code deposit gas (GAS_CODE_DEPOSIT * code_length) must have been charged, and the runtime code must be stored at the contract address.

The EVM execution loop must terminate: at every iteration, either an opcode is executed and pc advances, or a termination condition (STOP/RETURN/REVERT/error) halts execution. Infinite loops are prevented by gas exhaustion.
When an invalid opcode is encountered, execution must immediately halt with an InvalidOpcode error; all remaining gas is consumed.
The call stack depth must never exceed 1024 (STACK_DEPTH_LIMIT); any CALL/CREATE at depth >= 1024 must fail with StackDepthLimitError without executing the nested call.
All opcodes in the instruction table must be correctly implemented; incorrect opcode implementation would lead to consensus failures or security vulnerabilities.
Memory and stack operations must be bounded; gas costs for memory expansion must prevent host system resource exhaustion from unbounded memory growth.
MAX_CODE_SIZE and MAX_INIT_CODE_SIZE limits must be enforced to prevent code-size-based storage bloat attacks.

After a message call to an empty address, contract creation must be initiated; after a call to an existing address, regular message call must be processed. The call type determination must be deterministic.
When SSTORE clears a storage slot, the refund counter must be incremented; the gas refund must be correctly tracked across the execution frame.
Jump destination validation must be performed before execution for all JUMP and JUMPI instructions; the valid_jump_destinations set must be correctly pre-computed and immutable during execution.

After REVERT executes, all state modifications in the current execution frame must be rolled back, the error message must be available in the return data buffer, and unused gas must be preserved and returned to the caller.
REVERT must preserve unused gas unlike out-of-gas exceptions: only the gas cost of the REVERT operation itself (equivalent to RETURN cost) is consumed; the remainder is returned to the caller.
If insufficient gas remains for REVERT execution, the behavior must fall back to a standard out-of-gas exception which consumes all remaining gas.
When REVERT occurs during CREATE/CREATE2 init code, the contract must not be deployed (no code stored), and 0 must be pushed to the caller's stack to signal failure.
The return data buffer must contain the full error message after REVERT; the output area receives truncated data if out_size is smaller than the actual return data length.
Stack underflow during REVERT must consume all remaining gas, behaving identically to an out-of-gas exception.

Before executing a JUMP instruction, the destination address popped from the stack must be validated against the pre-computed valid_jump_destinations set; destinations not in this set must cause InvalidJumpDestError.
After a valid JUMP, the program counter must be set exactly to the validated destination address; after JUMPI with condition == 0, the PC must increment by 1 for sequential execution.
For JUMPI, the condition value must be evaluated as: non-zero triggers the jump, zero continues sequential execution. The condition is popped after the destination.
When InvalidJumpDestError is raised, all remaining gas must be consumed and execution must halt immediately.
The valid_jump_destinations set must be pre-computed by scanning bytecode for JUMPDEST opcodes and must be immutable during execution; runtime modification would allow arbitrary code execution.

Gas costs for control flow opcodes must be deterministic: GAS_BASE for PC/GAS, GAS_MID for JUMP, GAS_HIGH for JUMPI, GAS_JUMPDEST for JUMPDEST. Inconsistency across implementations would cause consensus failures.
After STOP opcode execution, evm.running must be set to False and execution must halt gracefully without error.

The wallet must display the validator address and data to sign to the user for explicit approval before constructing and signing the prefixed message. No signature must be generated without user consent.
After user approval, the message must be constructed as exactly: 0x19 || 0x00 || validatorAddress || dataToSign, then hashed with keccak256, then signed with ECDSA using the signer's private key.

When verifying a signature, the validator must reconstruct the message using its OWN address (not a supplied address), compute keccak256, and use ecrecover to derive the signer. The validator must never accept signatures intended for other validators.

The EIP-191 prefix (0x19 || 0x00) ensures domain separation: a signature created for one validator cannot be replayed at a different validator, because the different validator address produces a different hash.
The 0x19 prefix prevents signatures from being submitted as valid Ethereum transactions; the format mismatch ensures complete transaction replay protection.
Users must verify the validator address displayed by the wallet before approving; malicious dApps could request signatures for fraudulent validators.
Implementations SHOULD include chainId and nonce in dataToSign for replay protection; omission creates cross-chain and temporal replay vulnerabilities.

When receiving a NewPooledTransactionHashes (eth/68) announcement, the node must validate that the types, sizes, and hashes arrays have identical length; inconsistent array lengths must cause message rejection.
Before fetching a transaction, the node must evaluate the announced type and size against its policy: unwanted types or oversized transactions must be skipped without requesting full data.

Peers may lie about transaction types and sizes in announcements; after fetching full transaction data, the node must verify actual type and size match the announcement. Mismatches should affect peer reputation.
Nodes must implement reasonable throttling policies based on announced transaction metadata; without proper throttling, eth/68 size metadata provides no protection against bandwidth exhaustion.

After building a NewPooledTransactionHashes message, the types array must contain 1-byte transaction type codes, sizes must reflect the encoded transaction size, and hashes must be the transaction hashes. All arrays must be equal length.
Per-peer and global bandwidth limits based on announced transaction sizes must be enforced to prevent amplification attacks from large transactions (e.g., blob transactions).
